articles.author: Jesse Rogers
articles.title: Sources: Free agent Trevor Rogers, Cubs reach 5-year deal
articles.take: A straight news report with the important context: Rogers goes to the top of a rotation with almost no healthy starters, the QO costs two picks and $1M, and Hawkins expects most of the work after the lockout. It flags the ground-ball dip and leans on the Gold Glove defense. Solid and accurate, but it doesn't wrestle with the durability history.

articles.author: Jared Greenspan
articles.title: Cubs reach multiyear deal with lefty Rogers (source)
articles.take: The best quick read on why Rogers is better than his 4.03 ERA: the flu-wrecked start, the 2.90 ERA and 2.89 FIP over his last 20 starts, and the Driveline velocity rebuild. The deception and command case holds up. It undersells the Miami injury years, but the core argument is right.

articles.author: Bob Nightengale
articles.title: 'Sku-bino has fallen': Biggest MLB rumors we're hearing on the feeding frenzy
articles.take: A team-by-team notes column after Skubal. The Cubs item is the news: 'extensive talks' with Peralta, strong interest in Taira, and a goal of one or two free-agent starters before the lockout. The Webb note, that a deal is doubtful before Dec. 1 and may be tied to Adames, Chapman or Devers, is the most useful line in it. It's a notes dump, not analysis, and it misspells Peralta, but the reporting moves the board.

articles.author: Carson Wolf
articles.take: Good inventory: six departed starters took 106 starts, 617 1/3 innings and 5.8 fWAR with them, while the rest of the staff made 0.2. The ending falls apart. Rogers or Taira plus Holmes and Peterson is a rotation of No. 3s and 4s built on Steele's elbow, and calling Webb's price the reason to skip him ignores that the Cubs' spare young bats are the exact currency San Francisco wants.
articles.title: What's the Cubs' Plan for Their 2027 Starting Rotation?

articles.author: Alexander Rosquez
articles.take: Frames the choice correctly: Webb costs prospects but no long contract, Peralta costs only money and years. Then it stops short of picking. The clock it describes is the argument for doing both.
articles.title: Cubs Face Logan Webb Trade Decision Before Lockout

articles.author: Zachary Rotman
articles.take: The best Peralta caution piece out there, built on Sharma's reporting: his K rate fell to 19.7% in Tampa Bay and a .235 BABIP did the rest. That's a real reason to cap the years. It doesn't make him a bad target; it makes him a four-year target, not a five.
articles.title: MLB Rumors: Freddy Peralta-Cubs problem, Logan Webb's sky-high price and more

column.title: Rogers is the right first arm. He can't be the only one.
column.dek: Five years and $120 million buys the Cubs the best lefty left. A week before the lockout, the rotation behind him is still a problem.

p: Late Monday night, a few minutes before 11 p.m. Eastern, Jon Morosi reported that Trevor Rogers and the Cubs had agreed. Ken Rosenthal confirmed it and added the terms: five years, $120 million, pending a physical. That's $24 million a year for the best left-handed starter left after Skubal.

It's a fair price. MLB Trade Rumors projected five years and $115 million. The Athletic had four years and $84 million. The Cubs paid about $5 million over the MLBTR number, which is what it costs when Toronto is calling the same agent the same morning. Ben Nicholson-Smith reported Blue Jays interest in Rogers on Monday. The Cubs closed before it turned into an auction.

There's a real cost beyond the money. Rogers turned down Baltimore's $23.15 million qualifying offer, so the Cubs forfeit their second- and fifth-highest picks in next summer's draft and $1 million in international pool money. That's the tax for buying at the top of the market. It's worth paying for a 29-year-old starter. It wouldn't be for a reliever.

The 4.03 ERA in 2026 is the misleading number. Rogers carried a 6.84 ERA into June after a bad bout of the flu. From June 1 on, he made 20 starts with a 2.90 ERA and a 2.89 FIP, per MLB.com. That matches the rest of his Baltimore run: a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts in 2025 and a 3.16 ERA over 48 starts and 279 1/3 innings since the start of that year.

The improvement has a mechanism, which is what separates it from a hot streak. His fastball sat at 91.9 mph in 2024. After a Driveline strength assessment and a lower-body rework, it was back to 93.8 in 2026, and hitters are at .204 against it since 2025. His 5.6% walk rate ranked in the 92nd percentile. He doesn't beat himself.

And he took the ball. Thirty starts and 169 2/3 innings in 2026, both career highs. For a rotation that lost all five of its 2026 finishers and has Steele, Brown and Horton all coming off surgery, that matters more than the strikeout rate.

Rogers is not an overpowering pitcher. His 41.1% ground-ball rate is light for a park that boosts homers, and Wrigley's homer factor ran 106 over the last three years. The Cubs are betting their Gold Glove defense turns his fly balls into outs. That's a reasonable bet, not a sure one.

Durability is the other question. Thirty starts was a first. Recurring lower-body injuries wrecked his Miami years and cost him all but four games in 2023. Five years takes him through his age-33 season. Years four and five are where this deal could go bad.
Still, he's priced like a No. 2, and that's what he is. The problem is that right now he has to be the No. 1.

body.h: The rotation is still one arm short
p: Put Rogers at the top and look down. Edward Cabrera posted a 5.96 ERA and the front office won't promise him a spot. Justin Steele hasn't made a big-league start since April 2025. Javier Assad had a 3.63 ERA on a 4.92 FIP. Ben Brown is out until around midseason after neck surgery. Cade Horton is out until the second half at the earliest. That isn't a contending rotation with Rogers added. It's a contending rotation minus one.

Carter Hawkins said at the GM meetings that more than half of the Cubs' offseason additions could come after the lockout. Fine for the bullpen, the corners and Logan Webb, whose trade Bob Nightengale already called 'doubtful' before Dec. 1. Not fine for the second starter. The Japanese arms don't wait. Kaima Taira has to sign by Dec. 1 or go back to Japan.

Taira is the right second move. He went 1.36 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 146 innings in 2026, he costs no picks, and his price sits well below Rogers'. The risk is workload: 146 innings is his career high. As a No. 3 or 4, that's acceptable. Nightengale says the Cubs have strong interest. They need to turn that into a signature this week.

Peralta is the bigger swing. The Cubs have had 'extensive talks,' per Nightengale, and Craig Counsell managed him for six years. But his strikeout rate fell from 22.1% with the Mets to 19.7% with Tampa Bay, and MLBTR's five-year projection is a year too long. With Rogers in hand, the Cubs can make a four-year offer and walk away if someone goes to five.

Rogers alone is a B+. Smart target, fair price, real cost in picks, and he fills the most urgent hole on the roster. If Taira or Peralta follows by Dec. 1, the winter is a pass and the Cubs go into the lockout with a rotation that can carry the best offense in baseball. If Rogers is the only arm, they spent $120 million to fill one hole in a rotation that has three.
One night ago, the Cubs had zero starters and a week left. Now they have one, and the week matters more than it did.

items.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
items.note: Unanimous NL MVP. 45 HR, 41 SB, NL-best .942 OPS, MLB-best 10.6 fWAR. Hank Aaron Award, All-MLB First Team, Platinum Glove.

items.name: Seiya Suzuki
items.note: 131 OPS+, career-best 5.1 bWAR, Gold Glove finalist.

items.name: Alex Bregman
items.note: 5.8 bWAR, NL Gold Glove at third, All-MLB Second Team, ninth in MVP voting. Hitless in October.

items.name: Michael Conforto
items.note: 118 OPS+ on a minor-league deal.

items.name: Carson Kelly
items.note: 97 OPS+ and 1.9 bWAR from a catcher is a win.

items.name: Michael Busch
items.note: 106 OPS+ at first base. The walks carried him.

items.name: Ian Happ
items.note: 103 OPS+, 189 strikeouts, platooned by September.

items.name: Miguel Amaya
items.note: 98 OPS+, propped up by a .315 BABIP.

items.name: Pedro Ramírez
items.note: Held short together at 22. The xwOBA says he was lucky.

items.name: Nico Hoerner
items.note: 84 OPS+. The xBA says he deserved better; the glove is elite.

items.name: Matt Shaw
items.note: 102 OPS+ with a .303 xwOBA. Still looking for a position.

items.name: Dansby Swanson
items.note: His worst year as a Cub at the plate (90 OPS+). The glove saved the grade.

items.name: Ben Brown
items.note: 228 ERA+ over 68 innings before the neck gave out. Neck surgery Nov. 9; back around midseason.

items.name: David Peterson
items.note: 114 ERA+ after the June trade.

items.name: Shota Imanaga
items.note: 32 starts and a 112 ERA+. The 35 homers keep it from an A.

items.name: Matthew Boyd
items.note: 108 ERA+ in 22 starts, then two first-inning homers in Game 1.

items.name: Javier Assad
items.note: 3.63 ERA, 4.92 FIP. The defense did him favors.

items.name: Ryan Rolison
items.note: 135 ERA+ in middle relief from a waiver claim.

items.name: Colin Rea
items.note: 137 innings at a 97 ERA+. Exactly what he is.

items.name: Jacob Webb
items.note: Nine saves, eight blown.

items.name: Kevin Gausman
items.note: 4.83 ERA and 0.1 bWAR after the deadline deal.

items.name: Clay Holmes
items.note: 1.55 ERA over his first five starts, 8.24 over his last four.

items.name: Edward Cabrera
items.note: 71 ERA+, -1.4 bWAR, left off the Wild Card roster.

items.name: Jameson Taillon
items.note: 25 homers in 76 innings, -0.9 bWAR.

items.name: The bullpen
items.note: 28 blown saves, a third of inherited runners scored, 14 different save-getters.

items.name: Rogers signing (5 yr, $120M)
items.note: About $5M over MLBTR's projection for the best lefty left. Two picks and $1M in pool money is the real cost. Thirty starts in 2026 was a career first, so years four and five are the risk.

items.name: Crow-Armstrong extension (6 yr, $115M)
items.note: The reigning unanimous MVP at about $19M a year through 2032. The best contract in baseball.

items.name: Bregman signing (5 yr, $175M)
items.note: 5.8 bWAR in year one. Years four and five are the risk.

items.name: Conforto minor-league deal
items.note: 118 OPS+ for almost nothing.

items.name: Peterson trade
items.note: 114 ERA+ in 15 starts.

items.name: Hoerner extension (6 yr, $141M)
items.note: Paying a glove-first second baseman through his age-35 season.

items.name: Gausman trade
items.note: A deadline splash worth 0.1 bWAR.

items.name: Cabrera trade (Caissie + 2)
items.note: The No. 1 prospect for 80 innings of 5.96 ERA.

items.name: Holmes trade (Rojas)
items.note: A top-two prospect for nine starts, zero postseason innings, and he opted out.

items.name: Bullpen construction
items.note: Hoyer's own words: 'I did a poor job on the bullpen this year, full stop.'

items.name: Kelly option declined ($1.5M buyout)
items.note: The right call on a mutual option. It only stays a B if they re-sign him or find a real starter.

items.name: Suzuki qualifying offer
items.note: Paid off as planned: he rejected it Tuesday, so the Cubs get a pick after the fourth round when he signs elsewhere.

items.name: No QO for Happ
items.note: He'd likely have taken $23.15M. Saying no was the disciplined call.

items.name: No QO for Boyd
items.note: A 36-year-old No. 5 isn't worth the risk of an acceptance.

items.name: Rea, Harvey, Thielbar options declined
items.note: $2.5M in buyouts to clear three arms that didn't miss bats or didn't pitch.

items.name: Assad option declined ($3.3M)
items.note: Saves about $1M through arbitration and keeps a useful swingman. Small, correct, and an honest read of a 4.92 FIP.

items.name: Webb restructure
items.note: Same $2.5M guarantee and a 2028 option. Smart, small.

items.name: Orze waiver claim
items.note: A 5.66 ERA with no options left. A free look, nothing more.

items.name: Sitting out Skubal (per Sharma)
items.note: Fine at $450M and $50M a year. Rogers a day later shows the money had a plan. One more arm by Dec. 1 and it's a B.

items.name: Internal plan for LF, RF and C (per Hawkins)
items.note: Hawkins admits the risk: unproven corners to pay for 'proven guys in other spots.' Fine as a trade-off. It stays a C- until those proven guys exist.

items.name: Kanzler replaced (Ben Martin, farm director)
items.note: Fast, internal and sensible. Adding Rylan Domingues on the pitching-analytics side is the right department.

items.name: Wiggins, McCullough added to the 40-man
items.note: Protects the Detmers trade chip and a Double-A arm with a 27.7% K rate. Correct and routine.

items.name: This offseason so far
items.note: Rogers is a real starter at a fair price. One arm in a rotation that needs two, with a week left. Add Taira or Peralta and this becomes a B+.

items.name: Holmes reunion interest (per Hawkins)
items.note: They traded a top prospect for nine starts, he opted out, and the GM wants him back at a projected three years. Only a one-year swingman deal gets this off a D.

items.name: Justin Lawrence (likely minor-league deal)
items.note: Free Triple-A depth with a 5.34 career ERA and a walk problem. Harmless, and not the impact arm.

items.name: Missing the Mariners' starter sale
items.note: Seattle wanted a third baseman and a right-handed bat, the Cubs had both to spare, and Kansas City got Miller and Evans. Dipoto now says 'zero' more.

items.name: McDermott waiver claim
items.note: Free, uses an empty roster spot, 30.5% minor-league K rate. Also a 14.6% walk rate and no options. Depth, not help.

items.name: Bart waiver claim
items.note: An 82 OPS+ backup for about $3M is fine. As the Kelly replacement it's a D.

items.name: Roxby for cash
items.note: Optionable arm with a 94.6 mph heater for nothing. Smarter than another out-of-options claim.

items.name: Arias, Roberts non-tendered
items.note: Correct roster math. Leaves the backup infield thin.

grades.sub: Season grades for the regulars, the staff and the front office. Updated Nov. 24 after the Rogers signing. On game days this becomes a post-game report card.
grades.title: 2026 final report card

regressionNotes.571948: His ERA beat his peripherals by more than a run.
regressionNotes.592332: He pitched better than the ERA, but 11 homers in 50 1/3 innings did the damage.
regressionNotes.592791: xFIP normalizes homers. Taillon's homer problem (25 in 76 IP) was real.
regressionNotes.608324: xSLG .391 vs. .464 actual. The power is the part most likely to fade.
regressionNotes.650644: 1.72 ERA vs. a 4.13 xFIP in 36 2/3 innings. A swingman, not a late-inning answer.
regressionNotes.663423: A 15.8% K rate. That ERA belonged to the defense.
regressionNotes.663538: The one regular who was unlucky. A .296 xBA says the average comes back.
regressionNotes.664023: Small gap. The .218 is mostly him.
regressionNotes.665795: xFIP says unlucky; an 8th-percentile xERA says hitters crushed him. Don't bank on a big bounce.
regressionNotes.665804: A .315 BABIP for a catcher. Expect the OBP to slip.
regressionNotes.669020: Middle-relief ERA, back-end peripherals. Fine in low leverage.
regressionNotes.673548: The expected line is still well above average. Price him on that, not the surface numbers.
regressionNotes.676962: Still very good, just not 228-ERA+ good.
regressionNotes.691718: Even after the haircut, a .372 xwOBA is elite.
regressionNotes.699393: The largest gap on the team. Don't pencil him into a corner spot off this line.
regressionNotes.807713: An xSLG of .353. The pop isn't real yet.
